attempts.entry_title: Movement encoding across brain areas (Wang et al. 2025) on the Mesoscale Activity Map
attempts.summary: Most of the paper's main findings could not be tested in this data. How much movement explains activity across and within brain areas, whether neurons lead or follow movement, and decoding choice from video all need the video or its autoencoder embedding, which the cited dataset version lacks. Of the 106 sessions the paper used, 72 have no video in any version. The data do hold the stated scale of neurons and structures, and the mouse-specific pattern of choice decoding from jaw and nose markers appears, though weaker than reported. The paper does not describe its choice decoder, and the one used here was weaker, which may explain the gap.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Wang, Kurgyis, Chen et al. (2025) on dandiset 000363, which holds 174 Neuropixels sessions of 28 mice in a delayed-response task, with three DeepLabCut markers from the side camera. The version the paper cites has no video, the later version has it for only 34 of the paper's 106 sessions, and the paper's autoencoder embedding and end-to-end networks cannot be computed here, so only the unit counts and the clustering of marker-based choice decoding by mouse are tested; the other claims are blocked.

outcomes.statement: The analysis covers more than 50,000 neurons recorded in more than a dozen cortical and subcortical structures, simultaneously with high-speed video of orofacial movements.
outcomes.source: Main text, Introduction, paragraph 4
outcomes.quote: we analyzed recordings of more than 50,000 neurons, recorded in more than a dozen cortical and subcortical structures, simultaneously with high-speed video of orofacial movements
outcomes.notes: Over the 174 sessions, all with video markers, 272,227 units; unit_quality good 154,948 and classification good 69,453. With the 2 Hz filter on avg_firing_rate, 88,647 and 46,658, so after the filter the count is above 50,000 under unit_quality and below it under classification; the criterion holds when either count exceeds 50,000, and the count before the filter does under both. Only units with classification good carry a CCF annotation: the 200,922 units with an empty anno_name are exactly the classification unlabelled ones, so 92,769 of the 154,948 unit_quality good units have no CCF location and 62,179 have one. Counted without nesting, each annotated unit once in its major Allen division with isocortex split into ALM and other isocortex, the units fall in 13 structures (ALM, other isocortex, olfactory areas, hippocampal formation, cortical subplate, striatum, pallidum, thalamus, hypothalamus, midbrain, pons, medulla, cerebellum), each with at least 100 units, under both labels, with or without the 2 Hz filter, and over the 174 sessions or the authors' 106. That is more than 12 by one, and it rests on counting ALM and other isocortex apart, as the criterion's list of areas does; without the split it would be 12. ALM here is the isocortex units on probes targeted to ALM, so it may include neighbouring motor cortex; the margin is narrow. About 40 units are in names the structure tree lacks (parts of the dorsal lateral geniculate complex, in the thalamus), which adds no structure. The 16 areas of area2anno.json nest (Thalamus holds VM, VAL and MD; Midbrain holds SC, MRN, SNr and PPN); their top-level areas with ALM give 10, so they are not the count. Over the authors' 106 sessions, 90,324 unit_quality good and 42,259 classification good units (28,606 above 2 Hz). measured gives the unit_quality good count and the number of structures.
deviations: The 2 Hz filter uses the dataset's whole-session avg_firing_rate, not the rate over the included trials (Methods, Prediction of neural activity, 'Neurons with low firing rates (below 2 Hz) were excluded'); the count before the filter already decides the claim.

The paper names no quality label; both of the dataset's (unit_quality and classification) are reported, as the criterion allows. Units with unit_quality good but no CCF annotation count towards the neuron count and not towards any structure.

Structures are the twelve major divisions of the Allen CCF, read from the authors' structure tree in their deposit (mousebrainontology_2.csv and mousebrainontology_heirarchy_cortexMaskExclusions21_sc.xlsx), with isocortex split into ALM (units on probes targeted to ALM, as the code's get_single_area_inds) and other isocortex, the level of the areas the criterion lists; each unit is counted once. A layer name missing from the tree takes the path of its area.

deviations: The marker decoder is not described in the paper and its code is not public; the claims file's readings (a) five-frame window, 10 features, and (b) single frame, 2 features, were run with L2 logistic regression, the penalty chosen by inner fivefold cross-validation from C in 0.01 to 100 (the grid of the paper's code, functions_for_r2.calculate_auc). Correct trials only with 20-fold stratified cross-validation (Methods, Trial selection and cross-validation). The paper does not say how the AUC at a time bin is formed from the folds. The main reading averages the test-fold AUCs, as the Methods do for the other cross-validated measures (Methods, 'Defining choice- and uninstructed movement-modulated neurons using video-based choice decoder', 'The final AUC for each neuron is the average of the test AUC across all test-folds'; 'Epoch-averaged explained variance', 'After this, the folds were averaged'); one AUC over the pooled out-of-fold decision values is a variant. Both give the same outcome.

The AUC is computed every 20th frame (68 ms) from -1.2 s to the go cue and averaged over the 17 bins, an assumption made to keep the run within time (the paper decodes each time bin); a mean over bins changes by noise only. The trimmed epoch (-1.05 to -0.15 s) is a variant.

Marker outliers above five standard deviations of the frame-to-frame velocity are replaced by linear interpolation (Methods, 'We identified outliers by a five-sigma threshold on velocity across frames and imputed outliers from nearby frames'). No velocity is taken across the gap between two trial videos; a frame is flagged when the velocity into it is an outlier, so a single bad frame also flags the next one (median 8.7 frames per 10,000 imputed).

The main set is the 106 sessions the paper used, named in the authors' Fig. 6 and 7 file and matched by link-authors-deposit; the sessions that pass the clock check and all decoded sessions are variants and give the same outcome. Seven sessions fail the clock check (see findings), none of them among the 106. Since the main set comes from the authors' deposit, the claim's data field is set to with_labels in the claims file and it depends on link-authors-deposit.

Two sessions are not decoded, SC032_121719 (8 correct left trials) and SC066_041321 (4 correct trials with marker frames over the delay epoch, as markers exist for 7 trial videos only); neither is among the authors' 106.

For the 34 that have it, reading the side view alone takes more than an hour a session (1.4 h at the rate of the final run, 47 h for the 34; the timed rate varies from run to run) before any network is trained on four CPUs, so they are also too large to compute here. The authors' per-frame embeddings are not in their Zenodo deposit (session_latents.pkl holds 16 images of 120 by 112 pixels for each of the 106 sessions), and the Google Drive folder the code's README links has no DOI or fixed version, so the protocol does not allow its use (author step 1.4). The deposit's per-neuron explained variances and choice AUCs are the paper's own results, not data, and are not used. This claim trains a shared encoder on 40 sessions' video and compares it with the session-specific autoencoders and the markers.

findings.statement: In five sessions, sub-440959 (SC011) on 2019-02-24, 2019-02-25 and 2019-02-26 and sub-442571 (SC022) on 2019-02-27 and 2019-02-28, the DeepLabCut marker timestamps advance 3.4 ms per frame but the video frames are 6.8 ms apart. As deposited, the tongue is visible at 6 to 13% of the lick events, and no shift of the lick times within 1 s brings this above 0.49; stretching each trial's marker timestamps by 2 from its first frame puts the tongue at 99.9 to 100% of the licks. Their trial videos hold 934 to 946 frames (median per session), against 1864 to 1886 in the other eight sessions of the same two mice, although the trials last as long (median 4.83 to 4.90 s in all 13) and each video starts at its trial's start; the median over all sessions is 1904. The video in the later version holds the same frame counts and carries no timing (a starting time with a rate of 1.0, no timestamps), so the 6.8 ms spacing is inferred from the frame counts and the licks, not read from the video. The markers of these sessions are on a time base half as long as the trial table's, and nothing in the files shows it; any analysis of movement around task events in them comes out wrong.
findings.checked: The printed outputs show it. Cell 8: the tongue-after-go-cue contrast is negative in 5 sessions. Cell 10: as deposited, the tongue is visible at 0.063 to 0.132 of lick events; the best fraction at any shift within 1 s is 0.484; stretching the timestamps by 2 gives 0.999 to 1.0. These sessions have 934 to 946 frames per trial video, against a median of 1904. Caveat: 6.8 ms apart is inferred from the x2 stretch, not measured; these sessions have video in 0.231012.2129 (cell 14), which could confirm it directly. The rating is right: signals on different clocks, the marker time base half as long as the trial table's, and nothing in the files labels it. The short videos are visible in the data but do not reveal the timing error. Any marker-to-event analysis of these sessions would come out wrong, although none of them is in the authors' 106.

findings.statement: In sub-455219 on 2019-08-07 (SC026_080719) the tongue is visible at 60% of lick events: 214 trial videos match the licks and 117 do not, and the session has 539 trial videos for 630 trials, so some videos are probably attached to the wrong trials. The cause was not established.

Marker frames are missing for whole trials in two sessions: sub-484676 on 2021-04-13 (SC066_041321) has markers for 7 trial videos (49 s) of 550 trials, and sub-484674 on 2021-05-05 (SC065_050521) lacks them for 140 of its 354 correct trials. The files do not say so.

The version the paper cites (0.230822.0128) holds no video and no autoencoder embedding, the input of most of the paper's analyses. The later version 0.231012.2129 (65.7 TB) adds the raw electrophysiology to 169 files and the raw video to 71 of them (renamed +image, 28.9 TB), from 16 of the 28 mice; 34 of the 106 sessions the paper used for Figs. 6 and 7 have video and 72 have none in any version. Units, trials and markers of four sessions drawn at random are identical in both versions. The authors' per-frame embeddings are in no pinned deposit.

The marker timestamps step by exactly 3.4 ms within a trial (99.9% of intervals to the microsecond), a frame rate of 294 Hz, where the paper states 300 Hz; they look written from a nominal rate, not measured.

Units carry two quality labels, unit_quality (good or multi, no description) and classification (good or unlabelled, 1,852 NaN), and only units with classification good have a CCF annotation (anno_name is empty for all 200,922 unlabelled units), so 92,769 of the 154,948 unit_quality good units have no location. Question for the authors. The choice decoder of Fig. 6 (from the embedding and from single markers) is not described in the Methods and its code is in neither public repository. Which classifier, features (single frame or the five-frame window), penalty selection and time resolution were used, and was the AUC of a time bin averaged over test folds or computed over pooled out-of-fold predictions? This attempt used L2 logistic regression with a nested choice of penalty on one or five frames of one marker, an AUC per 68 ms bin averaged over the delay epoch; on the authors' 106 sessions the Calinski-Harabasz score of Fig. 6e is 6.4 to 6.8 with test-fold AUCs averaged and 7.6 to 7.9 with pooled AUCs, against the paper's 12.57, and the best single marker gives a response-epoch AUC of 0.75 against the paper's 0.88.

attempts.label: DANDI:000363
attempts.entry_title: Form, timing and behavioural matching of the response to ALM photoinhibition (Yang 2026)
attempts.summary: The paper's main findings on ALM photoinhibition held up in this data. In all five regions the early population difference lies mostly outside the choice and action axes, lick decoding rises after Go, and a difference remains after matching laser and control trials on lick direction and reaction time. Finer values matched only in part, among them the early decoding accuracies, the choice and action shares before the lick and the ratio to control-trial splits. In the example session the displayed plane held 70 to 97% of the early difference against 25%, by a computation the paper does not describe.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Yang (2026) on dandiset 000363, the Mesoscale Activity Map recordings of Chen et al. (2024), which the paper reanalyses. On the 112 late-delay bilateral ALM photoinhibition sessions it measures how much of the early laser-control population difference lies on choice and action axes fit on control trials, how lick decoding and the axis shares change from laser onset to the lick, and the population distance that remains after laser and control trials are matched on lick direction and reaction time.

findings.statement: The pinned version holds what the paper describes. 168 of 174 files have photostimulation trials, 112 late-delay bilateral sessions come from 19 mice, and the mice and sessions per region equal Table 1 of the paper under its stated rules. No recording is deposited twice (spike counts, trial counts and trial timing all differ). Every photostimulation trial has one onset event inside it. Spikes and trials share a clock (the ALM laser-control difference 20 to 120 ms after onset exceeds that before onset in all 99 sessions with ALM units), and licks and video share one (the tongue is detected in 97% of frames in the 50 ms after a lick against 40% at times shifted by -0.5 s, in all 112 sessions).
Four units in the late-delay sessions have spike times that are not in ascending order. Analyses that assume sorted spike times (binary search for counts) must sort them first.

The brain region of a unit is given two ways, as the probe's target in the electrode location (`brain_regions`, e.g. "left ALM", "right Thalamus") and as a CCF annotation per unit (`anno_name`), and neither is described as the region used for analysis. The probe targets reproduce the paper's per-region counts exactly.

The video keypoint series (jaw, nose, tongue) hold x, y and a likelihood per frame, with no detection flag or recommended likelihood cut. The tongue has likelihood of at least 0.9 in about 10% of frames and in no frame of the choice window on 82% of trials, so how missing keypoints are handled changes any analysis that regresses out tongue position.
In two of the 112 late-delay sessions the side-camera video does not span the trials to within 5 s, so some trials of those sessions have no keypoints.

attempts.entry_title: Movement-null subspaces in ALM and the medullary reticular nuclei (Hasnain, Han & Economo 2025)
attempts.summary: The paper's main findings on layer 5 extratelencephalic neurons, that they resemble other motor cortex neurons in selectivity and subspace preference, could not be tested, as the paper's own recordings are not public. On the reused recordings behind Figure 4, the session selection could not be recovered, leaving 5 ALM and medulla sessions where the paper has 16. Medullary movement-null activity explained less variance than movement-potent activity under only one of several readings, and medullary selectivity, similar null and potent variance in ALM, and ALM patterns absent from the medulla held in part. Prediction of medullary null activity from ALM and its lower dimension did not reproduce; the decoder as described overfit, and the paper leaves its method open.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Hasnain, Han and Economo (2025) on the Mesoscale Activity Map dataset, DANDI:000363, which the paper reuses for its Figure 4. It selects the bilateral ALM and the ALM and medulla sessions, then tests lick-direction selectivity in the medullary reticular nuclei, the variance in movement-null and movement-potent subspaces in each region, cross-region decoding of movement-null activity, the dimensionality of the movement-null subspaces and a joint UMAP embedding. The paper's own cell-type-specific recordings (Figures 1 to 3) are not public.

outcomes.statement: In the MAP dataset, the paper's selection gives 20 bilateral ALM sessions from 10 mice (961 right and 1055 left ALM units) and ALM and medulla sessions with 604 ALM units and 724 medullary reticular nucleus units.
outcomes.source: Methods, Curation of Mesoscale Activity Map Dataset (MAP); Results, A subset of null dynamics is found downstream of motor cortex, paragraphs 1 and 4
outcomes.quote: For simultaneous bilateral ALM recordings, we included 20 sessions from 10 mice, consisting of 2016 units (961 from right ALM and 1055 from left ALM). For simultaneous ALM and medulla recordings, we included 11 sessions from 7 mice, consisting of 1328 units (604 from ALM and 724 from medulla).
outcomes.notes: Reading G1 of 'good' (`classification`), units with a CCF label of MOs on a probe described as targeting ALM, or of IRN, GRN or PARN, and sessions with at least 30 such units in each region, gives 17 bilateral ALM sessions from 9 mice (paper 20 from 10), with 858 right and 1001 left ALM units (paper 961 and 1055; the left count is within tolerance, the right is not), and 5 ALM and medulla sessions from 4 mice (paper 16 in the Results, 11 from 7 mice in the Methods), with 300 ALM and 340 medulla units (paper 604 and 724). Only units classified good carry a CCF label, but the electrodes table gives each electrode's CCF coordinates, and among units classified good the nearest other such unit on the probe has the same label for 97.3% of units. With labels transferred that way (within 20 um), reading G2 (`unit_quality` good) gives 31 bilateral sessions from 12 mice (2767 and 2830 units) and 19 ALM and medulla sessions from 7 mice (1501 and 1745 units); within 0 um 28 and 13 sessions, within 40 um 35 and 22; reading U2 (all units) gives 44 and 28 sessions. G1 is the main reading for every Figure 4 claim (assumed). Its bilateral unit counts are near the paper's, where G2's are 2.7 to 2.9 times them, and the paper's 'classified as good' names the `classification` column.

outcomes.statement: Medullary reticular nucleus units are selective for lick direction in each epoch, most in the response epoch (sample 7%, delay 21%, response 49% of 724 units).
outcomes.source: Results, A subset of null dynamics is found downstream of motor cortex, paragraph 2; Figure 4b
outcomes.quote: Many units exhibited selectivity for either right or left licks in different task epochs, although selectivity was most prominent during the response epoch (sample: 7%; delay: 21%; response: 49%; n = 724 units Fig. 4b ).
outcomes.notes: 340 medulla units of the 5 G1 ALM and medulla sessions, correct trials, 54 to 136 trials per side per session. Under E1 with the Bonferroni threshold (p < 0.01) 32.4% are selective in the sample epoch, 49.1% in the delay epoch and 85.9% in the response epoch (paper 7, 21 and 49%). Under E1 the order holds (response highest, sample lowest) for every seed and both thresholds, so the claim is partially reproduced; under E2 the early delay sub-epoch (30.3%) falls below the sample epoch (32.4%). No reading puts a value within tolerance (E2 sub-epochs 30.3 to 66.8%; uncorrected p < 0.05 higher still). Over the five seeds E1 Bonferroni gives 30.9 to 32.9%, 47.9 to 51.5% and 85.0 to 85.9%. By session the sample value runs from 1.7 to 54.8%. The share of right trials changes over the session (0.13 to 0.73 by fifth in one session), but with labels shuffled only within blocks of 30 trials the values are 30.3, 47.9 and 85.9%, so slow drift does not explain them. Under reading G2 (1745 units, 19 sessions) the values are 16.7, 28.3 and 63.4% (16.6 to 17.6, 27.7 to 28.7 and 63.4 to 63.9 over the seeds), also partially reproduced.
deviations: Ignore, photostimulation and early-lick trials are left out, and so are trials whose sample cue does not start 1.85 s before the go cue (a 1.8 s or 0.3 s delay; 446 correct and error trials over the 22 sessions), as the epochs assume the paper's 1.2 s delay (assumed; the paper does not say how MAP's photostimulation, early-lick and other-delay trials were treated).
Epoch rates are the means of the smoothed 5 ms rates (Methods, "Identifying selective neurons"), not z-scored.
Units of reading G1 (map-session-selection); G2 is shown in the second notebook.

outcomes.statement: In MAP ALM the movement-null and movement-potent subspaces explain comparable variance (36.0 +- 7.40% and 37.1 +- 8.70%, mean +- s.d.; paired t test p = 0.15, 16 sessions).
outcomes.source: Results, A subset of null dynamics is found downstream of motor cortex, paragraph 3; Figure 4c
outcomes.quote: In the MAP dataset, the variance explained by movement-null and movement-potent subspaces in the ALM was similar to that reported here, with both subspaces explaining comparable amounts of variance (movement-null: 36.0 ± 7.40%, mean ± s.d.; movement-potent: 37.1 ± 8.70%; p = 0.15 , paired two-sample t -test; n = 16 sessions; Fig. 4c ).
outcomes.notes: 5 G1 sessions, 40 to 85 ALM units each. Under the main reading (W1, B1, D1, baseline z-score) the paired t test of null against potent variance finds no difference (V1 51.3 against 79.6%, p = 0.086; V2 23.2 against 36.9%, p = 0.125; V3 70.5 against 87.7%, p = 0.194), nor under W2 or D2, but no reading of M3 to M6 puts both means within tolerance, so the absence holds and the values do not, a partial reproduction. Under B2 the test finds potent above null (V1 p = 0.040, V2 p = 0.029), with means out of tolerance, which the criterion does not count against the claim. The z-score of example.m, a variant in the claims file, puts both V2 means within tolerance (30.2 against 29.0%) and there the test finds a difference (p = 0.028); were the variant a reading, the claim would be not reproduced. With 5 sessions the test has little power; the main-reading V1 difference is 28.3 points. Over the five seeds the main-reading V1 p is 0.079 to 0.086, the B2 V1 p 0.040. Under reading G2 (19 sessions) the main reading with V2 gives 33.9 against 42.7%, p = 0.251 (0.249 to 0.261 over the seeds), which the criterion counts as reproduced; the outcome rests on G1. G1 is held fixed for every outcome while the readings of M3 to M6 and the seeds are searched for one under which a claim holds; read the same way under G2, this claim would be reproduced. An earlier execution on a runner with other linear algebra kernels gave, under G2, 34.1 against 42.9%, p = 0.251 (0.251 to 0.266 over the seeds). Movement-null dimensions are 5 to 10, potent 4 to 9; 30 to 50% of bins are moving, mostly in the response epoch (51 to 82% of its bins, 1 to 25% of baseline bins).
deviations: 5 sessions where the paper has 16 (map-session-selection, reading G1, assumed); reading G2 shown in the second notebook. The selection is held at G1 while the other readings are searched, an asymmetry between the selection and the readings of M3 to M6, and under G2 this claim holds.

The movement threshold is Otsu's threshold on log10 speed, a standard choice for the value between the two modes that the paper set by hand; the keypoint positions are first smoothed with a Gaussian of 3 frames, as unsmoothed tracking jitter makes the speed histogram unimodal.
Ignore, photostimulation, early-lick and other-delay trials are left out (assumed).
The dimensions come from 100 shuffles of every 4th 5 ms bin, where the paper uses 1000 shuffles, to fit the time limit.
The readings W2, B2, D2 and the example.m z-score were each run with the others at the main reading, not in every combination.
The total covariance C of the variance explained is taken over the bins with tracking (no more than 0.1% of bins lack it).

outcomes.statement: In the medullary reticular nuclei the movement-null subspace explains less variance than the movement-potent subspace (26.4 +- 3.90% against 44.8 +- 7.12%, mean +- s.d.; paired t test p = 1.9e-9, 16 sessions).
outcomes.source: Results, A subset of null dynamics is found downstream of motor cortex, paragraph 3; Figure 4c, right
outcomes.quote: In contrast, in the medulla, the movement-null subspace explained less variance than the movement-potent subspace (movement-null: 26.4 ± 3.90%, mean ± s.d.; movement-potent: 44.8 ± 7.12%; p = 1.9 × 10 - 9 , paired two-sample t -test; n = 16 sessions; Fig. 4c , right).
outcomes.notes: Reproduced under the claim's seed with readings G1, B2 (supra-threshold runs shorter than 100 ms counted as moving) and V2, as the criterion accepts any one reading of M1 to M6. There the medulla null subspace explains 28.4% and the potent 51.9% (tolerances 26.4 +- 3.9 and 44.8 +- 7.12, so at most 51.92), paired t p = 0.017 over 5 sessions. Over the five seeds the null mean is 27.9 to 28.8%, the potent 51.0 to 52.3% and p 0.017 to 0.024; under the seeds plus 2000 and plus 4000 the potent mean (52.3%) is just outside tolerance, which would make the claim partially reproduced. V1 gives p = 0.003 with the potent mean (83.5%) out of tolerance. Under the main reading B1 the difference is not significant (V1 54.4 against 67.1%, p = 0.312; V2 34.5 against 41.4%, p = 0.344), nor under W2 or D2; the example.m z-score gives V2 p = 0.042 with the null mean (31.5%) out of tolerance. So the outcome rests on one of 15 reading combinations, which the paper does not settle, and under B2 the ALM difference is also significant (fig4c-alm-null-potent-similar): no single reading reproduces both Figure 4c claims. Under reading G2 (19 sessions) null is below potent under the main reading (V2 35.7 against 51.7%, p = 0.027; V1 p = 0.020; V1 and V2 p 0.008 to 0.027 over the seeds) and under B2 (V2 30.8 against 56.4%, p = 0.005), with the null mean outside tolerance in each, partially reproduced (an earlier execution on a runner with other linear algebra kernels gave V2 35.4 against 52.3%, p = 0.017, and B2 V2 31.3 against 56.0%, p = 0.0065). The combination that reproduces the claim is searched over M3 to M6 and the seeds with the selection held at G1; the same search is not applied to G2, under which fig4c-alm-null-potent-similar and fig4e-medulla-null-lower-dimension hold. 31 to 128 medulla units per G1 session.

5 sessions where the paper has 16; the threshold, trial, shuffle and covariance deviations of fig4c-alm-null-potent-similar apply.

outcomes.statement: Medullary movement-null activity is predicted from ALM movement-null activity (40 +- 8.1%, mean +- s.e.m.) nearly as well as contralateral ALM predicts ALM (54 +- 7.0%).
outcomes.source: Results, A subset of null dynamics is found downstream of motor cortex, paragraph 4; Figure 4d
outcomes.quote: Medullary movement-null activity could be predicted from ALM movement-null dynamics (40 ± 8.1%, mean ± s.e.m; Fig. 4d ) nearly as accurately as from the contralateral ALM (54 ± 7.0%, mean ± s.e.m; Fig. 4d ).
outcomes.notes: With lambda = 0.01, as the Methods give it, held-out R2 is far below zero under every reading (T1 or T2, R1 or R2, standardized or not), from -611.5 to -249.1% for ALM to medulla (5 sessions) and from -6098.6 to -2191.3% for ALM to ALM (A1, 17 sessions), against 40 and 54%; the values given as measured are T1, unstandardized, R1. It stays negative under the five seeds. The negative values are not due to the averaging or the denominator: the median over bins is -364.9 to -178.8% (ALM to medulla) and the R2 over the whole span, which keeps the time-locked variance, -320.8 to -120.3%. Nor do they come mainly from the heavy tails of the baseline z-score: with the example.m z-score (largest |z| 24 to 124 in the bilateral sessions, against 37 to 278) ALM to medulla falls to -1828.9 to -1512.9%. Over the 44 session and direction pairs the R2 falls with the number of predictors per training trial (Spearman correlation -0.61) more than with the source's largest |z| (-0.24), and it is above zero in 3 of 44 pairs, all with 0.24 predictors per trial or fewer: with up to 1.24 predictors per training trial (T1), a nearly unpenalized per-bin fit overfits. As variants with larger penalties, standardized and pooled, R2 is at most 16.6% (ALM to medulla, lambda 100), with ALM to ALM at 6.9%, below ALM to medulla, the reverse of the paper. The decoder amplifies differences in the last digits of the subspaces, which depend on the processor's linear algebra kernels: an earlier execution on another runner gave ALM to ALM -6039.6 to -2188.1%, the median over bins -364.1 to -178.8% and the span R2 -320.5 to -120.3% (ALM to medulla), and example.m -1829.2 to -1512.9%, with the same outcome.
deviations: Subspaces from the main reading and reading G1; the bilateral sessions are 17, not 20.
Larger penalties, the R2 over the whole span, the median over bins and the example.m z-score are shown as variants; the claim's lambda and the per-bin R2 of M8 decide the outcome.

outcomes.statement: Prediction is asymmetric; ALM movement-null activity is predicted less well from the medulla (21 +- 6.7%, mean +- s.e.m.) than the medulla from ALM (paired t test p = 1.2e-4, 16 sessions).
outcomes.source: Results, A subset of null dynamics is found downstream of motor cortex, paragraph 4; Figure 4d
outcomes.quote: ALM movement-null dynamics were less accurately predicted from movement-null dynamics in medullary reticular nuclei (21 ± 6.7%, mean ± s.e.m; p = 1.2 × 10 - 4 , paired t -test comparing ALM-to-medulla and medulla-to-ALM predictions; n = 16 sessions; Fig. 4d ).
outcomes.notes: Under every reading the paired t test of ALM to medulla against medulla to ALM gives p = 0.70 to 0.99 over 5 sessions, and medulla to ALM R2 is -517.9 to -290.4% (T1, unstandardized, R1 -491.4%), against 21 +- 6.7%; over the five seeds p is 0.45 to 1.00. Under the median over bins, the R2 over the span and the example.m z-score p is 0.11 to 0.99. In the lambda = 100 variant ALM to medulla exceeds medulla to ALM by 6.2 points (p = 0.091), with medulla to ALM at 10.4%. Under reading G2 (19 sessions) every mean R2 is below -10^6 % and p is 0.15 to 0.87, not reproduced. An earlier execution on a runner with other linear algebra kernels gave medulla to ALM -517.8 to -288.0%, the lambda = 100 difference 6.17 points (p = 0.094) and G2 p 0.197 to 0.987, with the same outcome.
deviations: As for fig4d-alm-predicts-medulla-null.

The example.m z-score, a variant, gives N1 10.2 against 14.4, p = 0.042. Under reading G2 (19 sessions) N1 does not differ (p = 0.98; 0.86 to 1.00 over the seeds) but N2 is lower in the medulla (3.35 against 5.93, p = 0.027, lower in 14 of 19; B2 p = 0.018), which the criterion counts as reproduced; there the medulla N2 is below 1.4 in 5 sessions, each with a unit whose |z| exceeds 3000. The outcome rests on G1, which is held fixed while the readings of M3 to M6 are searched; read the same way under G2, the claim would be reproduced under N2. outcomes.statement: In a joint UMAP embedding of movement-null activity, medullary units do not span the set of movement-null activity patterns seen in ALM.
outcomes.source: Results, A subset of null dynamics is found downstream of motor cortex, paragraph 5; Figure 4f
outcomes.quote: Further, examining a UMAP embedding of ALM and medullary movement-null activity, we found that the activity patterns observed in the medullary nuclei did not span the collection of movement-null activity patterns observed in the ALM ( Fig. 4f )
outcomes.notes: Test-set UMAP of 300 ALM and 340 medulla units (reading G1). 25.7% of ALM units have no medulla unit among their 10 nearest neighbours, against 0.1% with the region labels shuffled over all units and 0.1% with them shuffled within each session (21.3 to 27.3% over the five seeds), and 6 of the 26 grid cells that hold ALM units hold no medulla unit, so ALM holds patterns without a medulla counterpart, as the paper reports, and this is not clumping by session. The criterion's second part holds only in part. No medulla grid cell (0 of 20) lies outside the cells that hold ALM units, but only 59.4% of medulla units have an ALM neighbour (99.7% with labels shuffled within session; 58.2 to 62.6% over seeds). The medulla of sub-460436_ses-20200109 has d_null = 1 and its units spread along one line; without that session (claim seed plus 1) 21.0% of ALM units have no medulla neighbour, 16 of 57 ALM cells hold no medulla unit and 26 of 67 medulla cells lie outside the ALM cells. The judgment rests on these counts and the plots. The embedding depends on the last digits of its inputs, which differ between processors' linear algebra kernels, and an earlier execution on another runner gave 33.3% (23.3 to 33.3% over seeds), 3 of 28 ALM cells without a medulla unit, 2 of 27 medulla cells outside the ALM cells, 57.4% of medulla units with an ALM neighbour (57.4 to 65.9%), and without the session 20.1%, 20 of 62 and 20 of 62. Both executions give the same judgment.
deviations: umap-learn with the Methods' parameters stands in for MATLAB's run_umap (claims, M10); the neighbour and grid counts are this attempt's description of the embedding, the paper judges by inspection.
Units pooled over the 5 G1 sessions (assumed); subspaces from the main reading.

findings.statement: With the dataset's own CCF labels and `classification`, the paper's selection (at least 30 good units in each region) gives 5 ALM and medulla sessions from 4 mice, with 300 ALM and 340 medullary reticular units, where the paper reports 16 sessions (or 11 from 7 mice) with 604 and 724 units; and 17 bilateral ALM sessions from 9 mice where the paper reports 20 from 10. With `unit_quality` and CCF labels transferred by electrode coordinates from the nearest classified unit it gives 19 ALM and medulla sessions from 7 mice with 1501 and 1745 units, and 31 bilateral sessions. No reading of the files recovers the paper's selection.

The units' CCF annotation (`anno_name`) is filled only for units whose `classification` is good (69453 of 272227 units); the others have an empty label and only the probe's target region, though the electrodes table holds each electrode's CCF coordinates (x, y, z). The column description does not say this.

Units carry two quality labels, `unit_quality` (good or multi, no description) and `classification` (good or unlabelled), with no statement of how they differ; 1852 units have no `classification` value.
The jaw, nose and tongue tracking are stored with unit 'a.u.'; the values are pixel positions of the side camera (about 294 Hz, one segment per trial) and a likelihood.

The spike, video and trial clocks agree in all 22 selected sessions. The tongue becomes visible a median 56 to 262 ms after the go cue, lick direction is decoded from spike counts after the go cue well above shuffled labels, and jaw and nose speed rises at the go cue. The units of the session compared are the same in versions 0.230822.0128 and 0.231012.2129.

The trial table has no column for the delay duration. In the ALM and medulla sessions and the 2021 bilateral sessions used here, 13 to 57 correct and error trials per session (446 over 22 sessions) have a 1.8 s or 0.3 s delay in place of 1.2 s, which shows only in the sample and delay event times (`sample_start_times`, `delay_start_times`).

paper_notes.statement: The paper gives two counts for the ALM and medulla sessions of the MAP data (16 sessions in the Results and the Figure 4 statistics, 11 sessions from 7 mice in the Methods), two counts for the bilateral ALM units (1116 in the Results, 2016 in the Methods), and two decoding windows (the previous 40 ms in the Results, t and 8 preceding 5 ms bins, 45 ms, in the Methods).

Cross-region decoding (Figure 4d). With ridge lambda = 0.01 and the source projections at t and 8 preceding bins of 20 ms-smoothed rates, the predictors are nearly collinear and held-out R2 is far below zero on these data, falling with the number of predictors per training trial. Was lambda applied to standardized predictors, was R2 computed on held-out single trials at each bin and over which variance (the across-trial variance at each bin or over the whole span), and were trials or bins pooled before the fit?

Movement and stationary bins in the MAP data (Figure 4c to f). How was the hand-set threshold placed, were the keypoints smoothed before taking velocity, and do supra-threshold runs shorter than 100 ms count as moving? The medulla null against potent result here holds only when they count as moving.

MAP trials and units. Were photostimulation, early-lick and ignore trials used, and the trials with a 1.8 s or 0.3 s delay? Is the 'good' label of the selection the `classification` or the `unit_quality` column, with CCF regions assigned to which units? Here Figure 4c (ALM) is reproduced and Figure 4e is reproduced under N2 with `unit_quality`, and neither with `classification`.

Variance explained and dimensionality (Figure 4c, e). Which covariance and which d normalise the variance explained of each subspace (the reported null and potent values add to the total, which the Methods' formula does not give), and which measure of dimensionality, at which scale, does Figure 4e use?

The baseline z-score (Methods, Subspace identification) divides by the baseline s.d. across trials; for MAP units with near-silent baselines this gives values up to 278 s.d. among units classified good and above 50000 among units with `unit_quality` good. Were such units excluded, or was a floor applied?
